learningObjectives.title: Reactivity series and extraction of metals
Acids, alkalis, titrations and salt preparations

questions.q: Why are the Group 1 metals sodium and potassium stored under oil?
options: To prevent them reacting with oxygen and water vapour in the air
To stop them melting at room temperature
To keep them cool and prevent them evaporating
To help them dissolve slowly in the oil
questions.explain: Alkali metals are very reactive, so oil keeps air and moisture away from their surface.

questions.q: How does the reactivity of the Group 1 metals change going down the group from lithium to caesium?
questions.explain: Reactivity increases down Group 1 because the outer electron is more easily lost as atoms get larger.

questions.q: What is the collective name for the Group 7 elements?
questions.explain: Group 7 elements such as chlorine, bromine and iodine are called the halogens.

questions.q: What is the appearance of chlorine at room temperature?
questions.explain: Chlorine is a pale green gas, whereas bromine is a red-brown liquid and iodine a grey-black solid.

questions.q: Chlorine gas is bubbled through colourless potassium bromide solution. What is formed?
questions.explain: Chlorine is more reactive than bromine, so it displaces bromine from the bromide solution.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of clean, dry air is nitrogen?
questions.explain: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the volume of clean, dry air.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of clean, dry air is oxygen?
questions.explain: Oxygen makes up about 21% of the volume of clean, dry air.

questions.q: Which value is closest to the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide makes up only about 0.04% of the atmosphere.

questions.q: Which is the most reactive of these metals: potassium, copper, gold and iron?
questions.explain: Potassium is a Group 1 metal and by far the most reactive of those listed.

questions.q: A metal is more reactive than carbon. Which method is normally used to extract it from its ore?
options: It is found native and needs no extraction
Simply heating the ore in air
questions.explain: Metals more reactive than carbon, such as aluminium, are extracted by electrolysis.

questions.q: Why is gold found in the Earth as the uncombined (native) metal?
options: It is a liquid at room temperature
questions.explain: Gold is so unreactive that it does not readily form compounds, so it is found as the native metal.

questions.q: An iron nail is left in blue copper(II) sulfate solution. What is observed?
options: The nail becomes coated with copper and the blue colour fades
The nail dissolves and hydrogen gas bubbles off
A white precipitate forms in the solution
questions.explain: Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper, which coats the nail as the solution fades.

questions.q: What are the products of the reaction between an acid and an alkali?
options: A salt, carbon dioxide and water
questions.explain: Neutralisation of an acid by an alkali produces a salt and water only.

questions.q: To make pure copper sulfate from copper oxide (an insoluble base) and sulfuric acid, why is excess copper oxide added?
options: To ensure all the acid reacts, then the excess is filtered off
To speed up the evaporation of water
To make the salt insoluble in water
To act as a catalyst for the reaction
questions.explain: Excess insoluble base guarantees all the acid is used up, and the unreacted solid is removed by filtration.

questions.q: In a titration, 25.0 cm3 of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.100 mol/dm3 is measured out. How many moles of HCl is this?
questions.explain: Moles = concentration x volume/1000 = 0.100 x 25.0/1000 = 0.0025 mol.

questions.q: Which method is used to prepare an insoluble salt such as barium sulfate?
options: Mixing two soluble salt solutions so a precipitate forms, then filtering
Reacting an acid with an alkali and evaporating
Reacting a metal with a dilute acid
questions.explain: Insoluble salts are made by precipitation: mixing two soluble solutions and filtering off the solid formed.

questions.q: What is the test for hydrogen gas?
options: A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop
questions.explain: Hydrogen produces a characteristic squeaky pop with a lighted splint.

questions.q: A colourless gas is bubbled through limewater and turns it milky (cloudy). Which gas is it?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky, which is the standard test for the gas.

questions.q: What flame colour is produced by potassium ions in a flame test?
questions.explain: Potassium ions give a lilac flame, while sodium gives yellow, lithium red and copper green.

questions.q: Adding dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate solution to a halide solution gives a cream precipitate. Which ion is present?
questions.explain: With silver nitrate, chloride gives white, bromide gives cream and iodide gives a yellow precipitate.
